section.title: God Is Known in Judah
section.sectionRationale: A victory hymn of Asaph celebrating God's dwelling in Zion and His shattering of enemy weapons, likely tied to a sudden deliverance of Jerusalem, this psalm shows the God known in Judah as fearsome to nations yet a savior of the lowly.
section.thesis: The God who dwells in Zion is known by shattering the weapons of war and stilling the mightiest warriors with a single rebuke, so that every ruler on earth owes Him fear, vows, and tribute, for He alone saves the lowly and humbles the proud.
section.frameNote: Four movements: God known and near in Judah, verses 1 to 3; weapons silenced and warriors stilled, verses 4 to 6; fearsome judgment that saves the lowly, verses 7 to 9; a call to loyal worship and tribute, verses 10 to 12.

units.label: God known and near in Judah

verses.text: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A song. God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel.
His tent is in {{salem|Salem}}, His dwelling place in Zion.
There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war. Selah
You are resplendent with light, more majestic than mountains filled with game.
The valiant lie plundered; they sleep their last sleep. No men of might could lift a hand.
At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned.

units.label: Fearsome judgment that saves the lowly
units.note: the earth feared and was still

verses.text: You alone are to be {{yare|feared}}. When You are angry, who can stand before You?
From heaven You pronounced judgment, and the earth feared and was still
when God rose up to judge, to save all the lowly of the earth. Selah

units.label: A call to loyal worship and tribute
units.note: He breaks the spirits of princes

verses.text: Even the wrath of man shall praise You; with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself.
Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God; let all the neighboring lands bring tribute to Him who is to be feared.
He breaks the spirits of princes; He is feared by the kings of the earth.

salem.gloss: Salem, an ancient name for Jerusalem meaning whole, complete, or peace, the same root behind shalom. God's tent pitched in a place whose very name means peace shows His dwelling as the source of true and lasting peace.

yare.gloss: To fear, to hold in reverent awe. This is not mere terror but the fitting response of creatures before their Creator and Judge, a fear that in this psalm leads not to despair but to worship, vows, and tribute.

basic.context: A victory hymn of Asaph celebrating that God, dwelling in Zion, shattered enemy weapons and stilled an entire army with a single rebuke, likely commemorating a sudden, dramatic deliverance of Jerusalem from a besieging force.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm celebrates a specific act of God's deliverance while declaring an abiding truth: the God who dwells with His people is to be feared by every earthly power, and that same fearsome judgment is what saves the lowly.
basic.originalLanguages: God's dwelling in Salem, shalem, whose very name means peace or wholeness, verse 2, shows His presence as the true source of peace, while the psalm insists He alone is to be yare, feared, verse 7, a reverent awe that leads to worship rather than despair.
basic.typology: God's dwelling in Salem, the ancient name for Jerusalem also tied to Melchizedek, king of Salem, Genesis 14:18, anticipates Christ, our great High Priest after the order of Melchizedek, Hebrews 7:1-2, the true King of peace whose reign shatters every weapon of war.
basic.christ: The God who shatters weapons of war and rises to judge yet save the lowly anticipates Christ, the Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6, whose cross disarmed the rulers and authorities, Colossians 2:15, winning the ultimate and only lasting peace this psalm's Salem, city of peace, points toward.
basic.god: God is shown as both fearsome, unmatched in majesty and power over armies and rulers, and merciful, rising specifically to save the lowly of the earth, a judgment that terrifies the proud yet rescues the humble.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 7:1-2 ties Salem to Melchizedek, a type of Christ as King of peace and righteousness. Colossians 2:15 shows Christ disarming rulers and authorities, the ultimate shattering of every weapon raised against God. Luke 1:52 echoes this psalm's pattern of God humbling the proud and lifting the lowly.
basic.oneStory: This celebration of God's fearsome, peace-bringing power in Zion threads into the whole Bible's story of a King who dwells among His people and shatters every weapon raised against them, fulfilled in Christ, the true Prince of Peace who disarmed every hostile power at the cross.

context.literary:
The psalm is arranged in four short strophes, and each is marked by a different address. Verses 1 to 3 speak about God in the third person, 'His name,' 'His tent,' 'There He shattered.' At verse 4 the poem turns to speak directly to him, 'You are resplendent,' and keeps that address through verse 12 with one interruption. The move from report to address is the move from telling of a victory to standing in front of the Victor.

The middle strophes tell the battle backward. Verse 3 names the result, weapons broken. Verses 5 and 6 describe the result more closely: the valiant plundered, sleeping, unable to lift a hand, horse and rider stunned. There is no fighting scene. The psalm never describes a clash because in its telling there was none; God spoke a rebuke and the battle was over. The silence is the point.

The Selahs at verses 3 and 9 divide the poem into a local piece and a universal one. Verses 1 to 3 concern Judah, Israel, Salem and Zion. Verses 8 to 12 concern the earth, the lowly of the earth, the neighbouring lands and the kings of the earth. The verb 'fear' rings through, in verse 7, then in verse 8 as 'the earth feared,' and twice in the closing verses, so that the psalm gathers up awe as its main note.

Note how the poem turns from stillness to summons. The earth is 'still,' verse 8; the last verses order action: 'Make and fulfill your vows,' and 'bring tribute,' verse 11. The stillness of the battlefield becomes the stillness of worshippers who have nothing left to say but a vow. The final line remains on kings, 'He is feared by the kings of the earth,' rather than on Israel's safety, which shows that the psalm's real interest is God's honour among the nations.
context.historical:
The heading says 'with stringed instruments,' which places the song in the temple orchestra, and 'of Asaph' places it among the songs of the Levitical singers. The psalm names four places: Judah, Israel, Salem and Zion. Salem is the older name for Jerusalem, as the BSB footnote notes, and it was the city of Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18. Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where David's fortress stood, and in the psalms the name came to stand for the whole temple city.

Many readers connect the psalm with 701 BC, when Sennacherib of Assyria besieged Jerusalem after taking the cities of Judah. Isaiah told Hezekiah that the king 'will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it,' Isaiah 37:33, and 'the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians,' 2 Kings 19:35. Second Chronicles 32:21 adds that Sennacherib returned home in disgrace. The details match the psalm well: the 'shattered' arrows of verse 3, the warriors who 'sleep their last sleep,' and the strangely quiet battlefield.

The link is a reasonable inference and not a certainty, because the psalm does not name Assyria. The same city was also threatened by a coalition under Jehoshaphat, where the prophet told the people 'the battle does not belong to you, but to God,' 2 Chronicles 20:15, and the enemies destroyed each other. The psalm's language would suit either event, and the singers may have been glad to see it fit both.

Whichever occasion first inspired it, the psalm reflects Israel's belief about Zion. The temple hill was thought of as the place where God's name dwelt, so that an attack on Jerusalem was an attack on him. Psalms 46 and 48 make the same claim in songs of the same kind. A king coming against Zion, as verse 12 says, was coming against the God who breaks the spirits of princes.
context.canonical:
Psalm 76 belongs with the songs of Zion, Psalms 46, 48, 87 and this one. Psalm 46:9 says God 'breaks the bow and shatters the spear; He burns the shields in the fire,' and Psalm 48:4-6 tells how the kings assembled, saw, and fled in terror. The set of ideas is the same: God dwells in Zion, kings attack, God stills them without human help. Read after Psalm 75, where God says he will cut off the horns of the wicked, Psalm 76 shows a horn cut off.

The place of the psalm in Book III matters too. Most of the neighbours are laments over ruin, Psalms 74, 77, 79, 80. Set among them, Psalm 76 reminds the singer of a day when the city was spared, and gives the mourners something to remember. It serves as the memory of deliverance that Psalm 77 says the sufferer must deliberately recall.

The prophets took the same picture and stretched it to the end of history. Isaiah 2:2-4 sees the mountain of the LORD established, the nations streaming to it, and swords beaten into ploughshares. Zechariah 9:9-10 has the humble king who cuts off the chariot and the war horse and proclaims peace to the nations. Micah 4 repeats Isaiah. The pattern of Psalm 76, God stills the weapons in Zion and the nations come with tribute, is the pattern of the day of the LORD.

The New Testament reads the theme in Christ. Ephesians 2:14-17 says he is our peace, who tore down the dividing wall and preached peace to those far away and those near. Colossians 2:15 says he disarmed the powers at the cross. And Revelation 15:3-4 has the victors sing a song in which the nations come and worship, echoing verses 10 and 11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The singer wants the assembly to give the honour for a deliverance to the right person. There is no hero in the psalm except God: no king rides out, no army wins, no general is named. The credit is given wholly to the one whose rebuke stilled horse and rider. Anyone who sang it after a great deliverance was reminded that the victory was not theirs.

He also wants worshippers to hold awe and safety together. Verse 7 asks 'who can stand before You?', and verse 9 says the reason God rose up was to 'save all the lowly of the earth.' The same act that terrifies the proud is the act that rescues the humble. This is why the psalm calls the same God 'to be feared' three times and yet invites a joyful celebration in Zion.

Finally the psalm turns the memory into a command. Verses 11 and 12 tell the neighbours and the singers alike to bring vows and tribute. The author does not want the congregation to admire the victory and go home. He wants them to pay what they promised, and to make sure that the fear of the LORD becomes worship rather than mere relief.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a deliverance that God gave to a city he had chosen. It does not promise that every city under attack will be saved, and it should not be read as a guarantee that Jerusalem could never fall. The next generation of singers saw that it could, in 586 BC, and Jeremiah warned that trusting in the temple was a lie if the people would not amend their ways, Jeremiah 7:4. The psalm records what God did, not what he must always do.

What the psalm prescribes is plain. Fear the LORD, verse 7, make and keep vows, verse 11, and bring tribute to him. Those are commands that continue. The vow-making of verse 11 is not a call to bargain with God but to respond to what he has already done.

Military and political readings need care. The psalm celebrates the breaking of weapons; it does not authorise a nation to expect divine victory or to call its own wars holy. Its picture is of God acting alone, without any human sword. For Christians the application to the church is in Ephesians 6:12, where the struggle is against spiritual powers, and Zechariah 4:6, where the word is 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit.'

debates.question: What does verse 10 mean: that human wrath brings God praise, or that God restrains it?

views.label: God turns human wrath into praise
views.case: The BSB reads 'Even the wrath of man shall praise You; with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself.' God takes even hostile fury and makes it display his glory, as Pharaoh's anger did at the sea, Exodus 14:4, and as the Assyrian's pride served God's purpose in Isaiah 10:5-15.

views.label: God limits the wrath that remains
views.case: The footnote gives another rendering, 'Surely Your wrath against men brings You praise, and the survivors of Your wrath will be restrained.' On this reading the wrath is God's, the survivors are the remnant who are held in check, and the verse says that judgment produces praise.

views.label: The survivors are worshippers
views.case: Some read the 'survivors' as those who escape the battle and become worshippers, which fits verse 11, where the neighbours are told to bring tribute.

debates.bearing: All the readings teach that no hostility is beyond God's control. The choice affects whose wrath is meant, but not the comfort: the worst human anger does not finally escape his use.

debates.question: Which event lies behind the psalm?

views.label: Sennacherib's defeat in 701 BC
views.case: Isaiah 37:33-36 and 2 Kings 19:35 describe a sudden destruction of an army outside Jerusalem without a battle, which matches verses 3 to 6.

views.label: A different deliverance
views.case: The psalm does not name the enemy, and other threats, such as the one in 2 Chronicles 20, could equally be in mind.

views.label: A hymn of Zion applied to any deliverance
views.case: Like Psalms 46 and 48, it uses stock language of kings and armies against Zion, and later generations could sing it without a specific event.

debates.bearing: The theology is the same in all three. God defends the place of his name without human weapons, and his people are summoned to respond with vows and worship.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'fear' is the psalm's spine. In verse 7 the Hebrew says 'You, You are to be feared,' with the pronoun doubled for emphasis, and the same root returns in verse 11 for 'Him who is to be feared' and again in verse 12, 'He is feared by the kings of the earth.' In verse 8 the earth 'feared' as well. This is a fear that includes awe, reverence and terror, the reaction to a presence too great to manage. It is the fear that the proverb calls the beginning of wisdom, and it is the opposite of the fear of man. The psalm's point is that this one fear cancels the other kind.

In verse 6 the word for 'rebuke' is one used elsewhere for God's command over waters. Psalm 18:15 says the channels of the sea appeared 'at Your rebuke, O LORD,' and Psalm 106:9 says 'He rebuked the Red Sea, and it dried up.' The word describes a spoken command that the created order obeys. Psalm 76 applies it to the horse and rider, and the effect is the same: the object obeys and is still.

The verb 'stunned' at the end of verse 6 is the root of the word for deep sleep in the Hebrew Bible, the sleep that came on Adam when God formed Eve, Genesis 2:21, and on Jonah in the hold of the ship, Jonah 1:5. Verse 5 has already said the warriors 'sleep their last sleep,' and the two verses use the language of sleep for defeat. It is a grim irony. Men who should have been awake on the watch have been put to sleep by God.

In verse 8 the earth is 'still.' The verb is the one used in Judges 3:11 for the land that 'had rest for forty years.' In Psalm 76 the stillness is not the peace of a treaty but the hush that follows a divine verdict. The earth is quiet because the judge has spoken.

The 'lowly' of verse 9 is a word for the afflicted or humble, and Psalm 149:4 says God 'adorns the afflicted with salvation.' The word describes people who depend on God because they have no strength of their own. It is these, not Israel as a nation, whom God rises to save: the psalm's verdict is for the humble of the whole earth, not just those in Zion.

Finally, the double naming of the city in verse 2, 'Salem' and 'Zion,' gives the same place two names in parallel. The BSB footnote says Salem means Jerusalem. Salem is the same root as the Hebrew word for peace, and it brings with it the memory of Melchizedek, Genesis 14:18, and the meaning the writer of Hebrews takes from it, 'king of peace,' Hebrews 7:2.

typology.type: Salem, the dwelling of God, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: Salem was first the city of Melchizedek, king and priest of God Most High, Genesis 14:18-20. The letter to the Hebrews explains that his name means king of righteousness and king of peace, and that Christ is a priest for ever 'like' him, Hebrews 7:1-3. The correspondence is between a city of peace where God dwells and a king-priest who brings peace. The escalation is that in Christ the peace is made through his blood, Ephesians 2:14-17. The type falls short because the earthly city was still threatened by armies, while the peace of Christ is not taken away.

typology.type: Weapons broken without human hands, verses 3 to 6
typology.fulfillment: God stills the arrows, sword and shield with a rebuke. In Zechariah 9:9-10 the humble king comes on a donkey and cuts off the chariot and the war horse, and in Colossians 2:15 Christ disarms the powers by the cross. The correspondence is a victory won without a battle. The escalation is that the cross seems a defeat but is the triumph. The type falls short in that Psalm 76 destroys a visible enemy, whereas the cross defeats an enemy behind the enemies, and the full end of war still waits for the day when nations will not lift up sword against nation, Isaiah 2:4.

typology.type: Judgment that saves the lowly, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: God rises to judge in order to save. This is the shape of the gospel: the judgment falls on Christ and the lowly are saved. Mary's song, Luke 1:52, and Jesus' own words in Luke 18:14 carry the humble to exaltation. The correspondence is that God's justice and mercy are one act. The escalation is at the cross, where the just judge takes the penalty himself. The type falls short because in the psalm the judgment lands on human enemies, while the cross takes it on the judge's own Son.

typology.type: Tribute brought to the LORD, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The neighbouring lands are told to bring tribute to the God of Zion. Isaiah 60 and Psalm 72 picture the nations bringing gifts, and the magi who bring gold, frankincense and myrrh to the child in Matthew 2:11 begin the fulfilment. Revelation 21:24 says the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city. The correspondence is nations coming to honour the God of Israel. The type falls short because the psalm imagines tribute to a city, while the New Testament sees the nations coming to a person, and the city with no temple.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through the peace of Salem. The dwelling of God is in a city whose name means peace, and yet the city is a place where arrows must be shattered. The psalm therefore holds the question of how there can be peace in a world of weapons. The New Testament's answer is that Christ is Himself 'our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14. His peace is not a truce between armies but a reconciliation 'through the cross, by which He extinguished their hostility,' verse 16. Isaiah had named the promised child 'Prince of Peace' and said that 'of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end,' Isaiah 9:6-7.

It leads to Christ through the king who wins without a battle. In verse 3 the weapons are shattered 'there,' in Zion, by God. Zechariah 9:9-10 shows Zion's King coming humble on a donkey, breaking the bow of war and speaking peace to the nations, and the Gospels place Jesus on that donkey at the entry into Jerusalem. The psalm's cry that 'no men of might could lift a hand' finds its counterpart in the arrest in Gethsemane, where Jesus tells Peter to put his sword away, and the powers and authorities are disarmed at the cross, Colossians 2:15. The strongest weapons of the world are set aside by a man who submits to them.

It leads to Christ through the judge who saves. Verse 9 says God rose up 'to judge, to save all the lowly of the earth.' Judgment and salvation are the same act. On the cross the judgment on sin falls where God chose to put it, and the lowly are saved. The Gospel records the Roman centurion and the thief, both humble in different ways, as examples of who is saved when the Judge is on the cross. The earth 'feared and was still' as it did at His death, when the earth quaked and the veil was torn, Matthew 27:51.

It leads to Christ finally through the fear that becomes worship. Verse 11 asks for vows and tribute to 'Him who is to be feared.' In Revelation 15:3-4 the victors sing, 'Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name?' and the song is joined to the Lamb. The kings of the earth who are broken in verse 12 are also, in Isaiah 60 and Revelation 21, the kings who bring their glory into the city.

A caution: Psalm 76 does not speak of a coming Messiah, and the Melchizedek link belongs to Hebrews, not to the psalm. Its name Salem is a hint, but the reading depends on what the New Testament does with the name. The strongest connection is the pattern of victory by rebuke and peace by judgment, which the Gospels show in the person of Jesus.
study.god:
The psalm shows God first as known. 'God is known in Judah' is the opening claim, and the rest of the poem gives the evidence: what the community knows of God is what he has done in their city. God's self-revelation is tied to a place and to events, not to abstract ideas. Israel's faith is a memory of rescues.

It shows him as majestic. Verse 4 says he is 'resplendent with light, more majestic than mountains filled with game', hills rich in prey, where predators hunt and take their spoil. God outshines them. The comparison is a way of saying that all the strength of the natural and political world is small next to his brilliance.

It shows him as sovereign over war. The weapons are broken, the warriors sleep, the horses are stunned, and there is no struggle. Psalm 46:9 makes the same point: he makes wars cease to the ends of the earth. God does not need to fight as a human army fights. A rebuke is enough. This sets the psalm against the idea that power lies in weapons or in military strength.

It shows him as judge, and here the doctrine is subtle. Verse 7 asks, 'When You are angry, who can stand before You?' That echoes the question about who can endure the day of his coming. And yet the judgment in verse 9 is directed toward the salvation of the lowly. His anger is not blind; it has a target and a purpose. Nahum 1:6 asks the same question, and Romans 8:1 answers it for those in Christ.

It shows him as one who uses everything. Verse 10, however it is translated, says that even the wrath of man ends up praising him. God is not merely one player among others but the one in whose hands the outcomes rest. Human rage is not a rival to his plan. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, Genesis 50:20, and the same principle runs through the psalm.

It shows him as one who must be honoured. Verse 11 turns to duty: vows are to be made and kept, and tribute is to be brought. The God who defends his people is also the God who calls for their allegiance, and a nation that receives his protection owes him its worship.

For worship, the psalm asks the congregation to sing with both trembling and gladness. It gives them a God who is to be feared and to whom they can bring their vows. It also lets the humble hear that the terror of judgment is on their side, because the one who rises to judge rises to save.

crossReferences.note: God brings devastation on the earth and makes wars cease, breaking the bow, shattering the spear and burning the shields. Together with Psalm 76:3, it shows the two songs of Zion describing the same act of God from slightly different angles.

The kings assembled, saw and fled in terror, seized by trembling like a woman in labour. It gives the human side of the fear that Psalm 76 describes from God's side, and confirms that the two psalms belong to the same tradition.

Isaiah's word to Hezekiah promises that the Assyrian will not shoot an arrow into the city, and the angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 men in one night. This is the likeliest historical setting for the stillness of verses 5 and 6.
Jehoshaphat is told the battle is not his but God's, and that he need only stand still and watch. The line shows the same theology of a victory the people do not win with their own hands.

Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blessed Abram. It is the first mention of Salem and explains why the psalm's mention of Salem carries the memory of a priest-king and the blessing of God Most High.

The writer explains Melchizedek's name as king of righteousness and king of peace, and presents him as a picture of the Son of God who remains a priest for all time. It shows how Salem's name becomes a sign of Christ's kingdom.
God rebuked the Red Sea and it dried up. The same verb of rebuke in Psalm 76:6 puts horse and rider under the authority that once commanded the sea, and links this victory to the Exodus.

Assyria is the rod of God's anger who boasts as though his own strength had won, and God says the axe cannot boast over the one who swings it. It is a long commentary on how the wrath of man ends by praising God, as in verse 10.
Zion's humble king comes on a donkey, cuts off the chariot and the war horse, breaks the bow and speaks peace to the nations. It is the fulfilment in prophecy of the weapons broken in Zion.

Christ is our peace, who has broken down the dividing wall and reconciled both groups to God through the cross. It shows how the peace of Salem is made real, not by shattering enemies but by making them one.

At the cross Christ disarmed the powers and authorities and triumphed over them. It gives the ultimate meaning of 'the shield and sword and weapons of war' being shattered, as the spiritual armies of evil are the last to fall.

Those who conquered sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb: who will not fear You, Lord, for all nations will come and worship. It carries the fear and worship of Psalm 76:7-12 into the final song of the redeemed.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 76 gathers a great deal of the Bible's plot into twelve verses. The story begins with a world that God made 'very good' and with a human race that turned toward violence. By the time of the flood the earth was 'filled with violence,' Genesis 6:11. From Cain onward, weapons multiply, and the great empires of the Old Testament are in the end armies. The psalm sets the God of Israel, who dwells in a small city, against that entire history of force.

The second thread is the promise of a place. Salem first appears in Genesis 14, where Melchizedek blesses Abram. David takes Jerusalem, Solomon builds the temple, and Zion becomes the place where God's name is said to live. The psalm sings about that promise in the good days, when the city was spared. Yet the prophets say the name is not a charm. Jeremiah warns that the temple will not save a disobedient people, and Babylon does what Assyria could not. The psalm is therefore both an assurance and a warning: the God who breaks weapons is the God who can also let the city fall.

The story then turns. The hope of the prophets is that the peace of Salem will one day cover the earth. Isaiah 2:2-4 sees swords made into ploughshares, Zechariah 9:10 sees the war horse cut off, and Isaiah 9:6-7 sees a child called Prince of Peace. The Gospels announce that this child has come, and that the peace he brings is made at the cost of his own body. Paul says that he has killed the hostility, Ephesians 2:16, and Colossians 2:15 says the powers were disarmed. The psalm's shattered weapons are seen in a fresh light.

The church now lives in the time between the cross and the end. It still sees weapons and kings, and it is tempted to trust them. Psalm 76 teaches it to fear the right one. It also gives it a mission: vows are to be kept, and the nations are to be invited to bring their tribute, which in the New Testament means being gathered into the family of God.

The story ends where the psalm points. Revelation shows the nations coming into the city, and the kings of the earth bringing their glory, Revelation 21:24. There is no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, and there is no more war, because the last enemy is defeated. The wrath of man has finally been turned to praise, and those who survived the wrath of God are clothed in his righteousness. The city of Salem, the city of peace, becomes the new Jerusalem in which God dwells among his people.

quiz.q: Where is God's dwelling place, according to verses 1-2?

options.text: His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion.
options.note: This grounds the psalm's celebration in God's own chosen dwelling among His people.

options.text: In a temple built in Egypt.
options.note: The text names Salem and Zion, not Egypt.

options.text: Nowhere in particular; God is only in heaven.
options.note: The psalm specifically emphasizes God's dwelling among His people in Salem and Zion, not only a distant heaven.

options.text: In the wilderness, far from any city.
options.note: The text is explicit that His dwelling is in Salem and Zion, a city, not the wilderness.

quiz.q: What did God shatter there, according to verse 3?

options.text: The flaming arrows, shield, sword, and weapons of war.
options.note: This is the psalm's central picture of God's decisive victory over armed enemies.

options.text: The mountains surrounding Jerusalem.
options.note: The text specifies weapons of war, not mountains.

options.text: The idols of neighboring nations.
options.note: While God does oppose idolatry elsewhere, this verse specifically names weapons of war.

options.text: The city walls of Jerusalem itself.
options.note: The text describes enemy weapons being shattered, not the city's own walls.

quiz.q: What happens to the enemy army at God's rebuke, verses 5-6?

options.text: The valiant lie plundered and both horse and rider are stunned, unable to lift a hand.
options.note: A single rebuke from God renders the entire army powerless without a human hand raised against them.

options.text: They surrender peacefully after negotiations.
options.note: No negotiation is described; the army is supernaturally stilled by God's rebuke.

options.text: They retreat after a long siege.
options.note: The text describes sudden, supernatural stillness, not a prolonged siege and retreat.

options.text: They convert and join Israel's army.
options.note: No such conversion is mentioned; the army is simply rendered powerless.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of God's rising up to judge, according to verse 9?

options.text: To save all the lowly of the earth.
options.note: God's fearsome judgment is explicitly aimed at rescuing the humble and oppressed.

options.text: To destroy the whole earth without exception.
options.note: The text specifically names saving the lowly as the purpose, not total destruction.

options.text: To reward only the wealthy and powerful.
options.note: The opposite; God's judgment specifically favors the lowly, not the powerful.

options.text: To establish a new covenant with foreign kings.
options.note: The text describes judgment aimed at saving the lowly, not establishing covenants with foreign rulers.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's picture of God dwelling in Salem connect to the New Testament?

options.text: Salem is tied to Melchizedek, a type of Christ as our great High Priest and King of peace, Hebrews 7:1-2.
options.note: This is a direct typological connection drawn out explicitly in Hebrews.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of Jerusalem's future rebuilding.
options.note: The psalm makes no such specific prediction.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: Its Salem imagery is directly picked up in Hebrews 7 regarding Christ as the true Melchizedek.

options.text: It teaches that God no longer dwells among His people.
options.note: The opposite; the psalm and its fulfillment in Christ emphasize God's ongoing dwelling with His people.

questions: This psalm celebrates God's dwelling among His people in Salem, whose name means peace, verse 2. Where do you most need to experience God's peace in the middle of conflict right now?
God stills an entire army with a single rebuke, without a human hand raised, verses 5-6. What battle in your life do you need to entrust entirely to God rather than fighting in your own strength?

God's fearsome judgment is aimed specifically at saving the lowly of the earth, verse 9. Where do you need to trust that God's justice is ultimately good news for the humble, even when it feels frightening?
The psalm calls worshipers to make and fulfill their vows to the Lord, verse 11. What vow or commitment to God do you need to renew or finally keep?

Salem points forward to Christ, our true King of peace who disarmed every hostile power at the cross, Colossians 2:15. What hostile power, whether fear, sin, or circumstance, do you need to remember Christ has already disarmed?

translationNotes.note: 'Salem' is an ancient, shorter name for Jerusalem, also used in Genesis 14:18 of Melchizedek, king of Salem, and built from the same Hebrew root as shalom, peace.

The second half of this verse is difficult in Hebrew and can also be rendered 'Surely Your wrath against men brings You praise, and the survivors of Your wrath will be restrained,' shifting the emphasis from God repurposing wrath to God limiting it.
